name: Dermachrome Flush — The Visible Chrome Maximalism Wave
creator: Ironbloom Annex chrome artists; codified by stylist Orinthia Mwangi-Castellanos
description: A deliberate, joyful, and politically charged rejection of the earlier Dermachrome Null concealment aesthetic, Dermachrome Flush celebrates exposed augmentation hardware as beauty, identity, and defiance. Practitioners polish, paint, engrave, and illuminate their chrome — joint housings lacquered in vivid pigments, subdermal port rings set with decorative surrounds, neural interface studs crowned with hand-worked metalwork drawing on Yoruba, Mughal, Byzantine, and Māori ornamental traditions simultaneously. The movement insists that chrome is not a wound to be hidden but a biography written in metal.
medium: physical body modification; chrome-work studios; neural feed documentation; Chromesong circuit events
cultural_impact: Dermachrome Flush reframed augmentation — particularly the involuntary or economically compelled chrome common on the Shelf — as something to be claimed rather than mourned. Its aesthetic vocabulary, particularly the ornamental port surrounds, became the dominant chrome-display language across all tiers within a decade, though Spire adoption was largely stripped of the movement's political content.
controversy: Corponation augmentation manufacturers initially opposed decorative modification of their hardware as voiding warranties and obscuring diagnostic access. The counter-argument that workers owned their own bodies produced one of the defining labor-rights confrontations of the 2200s. Some within the movement accused Tier 4-5 adopters of wearing chrome pride as costume while supporting the mandatory augmentation policies that made Shelf chrome involuntary.
story_hooks: A chrome artist famous for intricate port-surround work in Igbo geometric patterns is offered a Spire commission — and must decide what it means to bring the movement's symbols into spaces of power.

A corponation technician discovers that a worker's decorative lacquer is actually concealing a hardware modification that bypasses the company's augmentation monitoring — the art was always the cover.
Two factions of the Flush movement are in open conflict: one wants to license the aesthetic to a major fashion house to fund Shelf chrome clinics; the other considers this a terminal betrayal.
